From Interaction to Capability:
Task Advancement as State and Supervision for GUI Agents

Ziyang Chen Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Qian Li Affiliation: Joint SDU-NTU Centre for Artificial Intelligence Research (C-FAIR)Shandong University    Chengwei Qin Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
Abstract

GUI memory should preserve the results of past actions and learn reusable operations. This is difficult in long-horizon workflows, where agents must use information across applications and useful operations are interleaved with failed attempts. We introduce Task Advancement Memory (TAM), which defines task advancement as verified task progress, and supports ongoing task execution and learns reusable operations. During execution, Task Advancement State represents how verified task progress changes the remaining goals, allowing the agent to build on earlier achievements across applications. After each task, advancement supervision identifies and abstracts the interactions that produced a verified local result. The learned operations preserve the relation between required inputs, expected outcomes, and verification conditions. This retains locally successful operations from both successful and failed tasks. On MobileWorld GUI-only tasks, Advancement State alone raises success from 12.0% to 28.2%. Full TAM achieves a 17.6% relative gain in task success over the strongest evaluated baseline and reduces lifecycle tokens per solved task by 38.7%. On SPA-Bench, TAM achieves state-of-the-art task success in the single-app English Level 3 setting.

1 Introduction

GUI agents should complete workflows whose information and effects are distributed across screens and applications. Long interaction histories mix completed work with attempts and productive actions with detours, leaving the agent to reconstruct how far the task has advanced and what remains to be done. For example, after confirming a calendar event, an agent should proceed to notifying participants using the event details it has already read. Therefore, memory should represent how completed work changes the remaining task.

Recent methods improve the information available to the agent through context management, program-guided execution, and verified task state (Yang et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Zheng et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b). Trajectory exemplars, induced workflows, and experience memories also transfer knowledge to later tasks (Zheng et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025a; Xiao et al., 2026; Ouyang et al., 2026). These approaches address how memory can help an agent complete remaining goals and how successful interactions can become reusable operations. However, agents still struggle to apply correctly acquired information to later goals across applications. Workflow memories tied to historical action sequences also leave the agent to adapt past routes when the interface changes. A task’s final outcome also gives incomplete feedback about intermediate operations, a failed task can contain useful successes, while a successful task can include ineffective attempts.

We propose Task Advancement Memory (TAM), a memory framework that uses task progress to guide execution and learning. A task advancement occurs when GUI observations confirm that a previously unresolved requirement is satisfied, either by obtaining required information or by achieving a requested outcome. Each advancement reduces what the agent still needs to determine or accomplish. We call this task reduction. For online execution, Task Advancement State makes earlier advancements usable by later goals. It shows what information is available for each remaining goal and which goals are ready to pursue. TAM uses each advancement to supervise the selection and abstraction of productive interactions. The learned operations specify the inputs needed at entry, the result to achieve, and how to verify it. This retains useful capabilities from productive portions of both successful and failed workflows. Figure 1 illustrates these two uses of task advancement.

We evaluate TAM on the GUI-only subset of MobileWorld (Kong et al., 2026) and the Level-3 English subset of SPA-Bench (Chen et al., 2025). With Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct used by every listed MobileWorld method, TAM improves success from 29.1% for the strongest evaluated memory baseline to 34.2%. With GPT-4o in the SPA-Bench English Level 3 setting, it reaches 57.0%, the highest success rate in the reported comparison. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We introduce Task Advancement State within TAM to guide execution across applications. It represents the remaining task in terms of satisfied requirements, available inputs, and unresolved dependencies. This lets the agent build on earlier advancements when choosing its next action.

  • •

    We propose advancement supervision, which converts partial task success into capabilities that can be reused in subsequent tasks. Each learned operation specifies what it needs, what it should achieve, and how to verify the outcome.

  • •

    We show that TAM outperforms the evaluated memory baselines in task success on MobileWorld and SPA-Bench. Cross-benchmark comparisons, component ablations, and cost analyses establish the value of task-state memory and the additional benefit of persistent operators.

2 Related Work

Task state and verified execution.

Explicit task representations preserve information and unfinished work across interface changes. AgentProg represents task variables and control flow; ATMem maintains task-driving information and execution status; TSR separates durable task information from transient observations; and StructAgent combines requirements, values, evidence, and verified transitions (Tian et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Zheng et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). MGA also organizes interaction around validated state changes (Cheng et al., 2025). These methods preserve explicit task information and distinguish intended actions from observed outcomes. TAM links task results to the remaining requirements they support. These dependencies guide execution and define the inputs and outcomes of reusable operations.

Trajectory, workflow, and skill memory.

Persistent experience can guide later tasks through demonstrations, trajectories, workflows, or skills. Synapse retrieves abstracted trajectories as in-context exemplars; AWM induces workflows from offline or online experience; and ReasoningBank distills reusable reasoning strategies (Zheng et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025b; Ouyang et al., 2026). Mobile-Agent-E stores tips and shortcuts, UI-Mem organizes workflows, subtask skills, and failure patterns, and SkillGen synthesizes and validates skills from successful and unsuccessful trajectories (Wang et al., 2025a; Xiao et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026). These systems reuse experience at different granularities. They adopt different rules for locating a reusable segment, assigning local credit, and verifying the result that the segment is expected to achieve. TAM selects interactions by the local requirement they satisfy and carries that requirement into the learned operation’s expected outcome and verification condition.

Exploration-built interface knowledge.

Another family constructs persistent knowledge through dedicated exploration. AppAgent builds application knowledge from exploration or demonstrations; GUI-Xplore learns action-aware structure from exploration videos; GUI-explorer generates function-aware exploration goals and mines transition knowledge; ActionEngine builds state-machine memory with an offline crawler; and EAM constructs an executable GUI graph through state-aware exploration (Zhang et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2026; Qin et al., 2026). This approach can provide broad interface coverage before downstream tasks are attempted.

3 Method

TAM uses task advancement in two ways. Task Advancement State represents what remains to be done using the information already obtained. Advancement supervision learns reusable operations from interactions that satisfy a task requirement. These memories guide a fixed base policy, which chooses primitive actions from the live interface (Figure 2). Appendix A gives the execution procedure, update rules, and learning details.

3.1 Task Advancement as a Shared Memory Unit

At step tt, a base policy πθ\pi_{\theta} receives the instruction gg, current GUI observation oto_{t}, bounded recent history HtH_{t}, and TAM’s bounded memory context CtC_{t}. It emits a primitive action in the original environment action space. TAM changes the supplied memory, without retraining the policy. A separate episode record 𝒯\mathcal{T} retains evidence for task-end review. Online state acceptance guides the current task, retrospective review evaluates which interactions should enter persistent memory.

At task initialization, an LLM-based task compiler identifies the information to acquire and the outcomes to establish from the instruction. It represents them in a graph 𝒬=(V,EQ)\mathcal{Q}=(V,E_{Q}), whose nodes VV are requirements and whose edges EQE_{Q} encode their dependencies. For each requirement qq, its dependencies RqR_{q} identify the requirements that supply its inputs, and an evidence rule VqV_{q} specifies how its result is recognized. An optional branch condition γq\gamma_{q} specifies when the instruction requires qq. These dependencies concern task results rather than a prescribed sequence of GUI actions. The task-local state StS_{t} records each requirement’s status, known values, and supporting evidence at step tt. Object bindings associate a value or outcome with its task entity, such as the event to which a meeting time belongs.

A task advancement records progress on a requirement: GUI observations confirm that previously missing information has been obtained or a requested outcome has been achieved. Let S−S^{-} and S+S^{+} denote the task memory states before and after an evidence update. Write zq±=zS±​(q)z_{q}^{\pm}=z_{S^{\pm}}(q) for the status of qq, with U\mathrm{U} and E\mathrm{E} denoting unresolved and established. An advancement is

Adv(q)=[(zq−,zq+)=(U,E)]Vq(ξ),\operatorname{Adv}(q)=\mathbf{1}\!\left[(z_{q}^{-},z_{q}^{+})=(\mathrm{U},\mathrm{E})\right]V_{q}(\xi), (1)

where ξ\xi is the supporting observation and Vq​(ξ)∈{0,1}V_{q}(\xi)\in\{0,1\} indicates whether TAM accepts it as evidence that qq is satisfied. Model-based extraction assesses the observed fact or effect; schema and evidence-reference checks associate it with the specified requirement. A single screen can establish several requirements. Each advancement also identifies a candidate interaction segment for later review and learning.

3.2 Advancement as State: Online Task Reduction

Task Advancement State turns verified progress into an explicit representation of the remaining problem. Information already obtained is bound to the requirements that need it, and satisfied requirements are removed from the remaining work. We call this task reduction. We call the unfinished requirements with their available inputs the residual task. Completed requirements leave this view, while their results remain in StS_{t} for later use. For example, Figure 2 assumes a departure time of 5 PM. Reading a driving duration of 3 h 18 min supplies the missing value for calculating arrival at 8:18 PM. The remaining goal is to send Susan that time. TAM thus carries the result of the route query into the messaging goal across the application change.

Reason from the reduced task.

Among the remaining requirements, TAM identifies those whose inputs are already available and whose branch conditions hold. This set is the Advancement Frontier. Let KtK_{t} and UtU_{t} denote the established and unresolved requirements, treating an absent branch condition as true:

Ft={q∈Ut:Rq⊆Kt,St⊧γq}.F_{t}=\{q\in U_{t}:R_{q}\subseteq K_{t},\ S_{t}\models\gamma_{q}\}. (2)

TAM uses the frontier to select evidence and operators relevant to this continuation. The actor uses the residual task and live screen to choose its next action, with earlier information already supplied to the requirements that need it.

Ground reductions in observed results.

TAM updates source information from the current observation and checks relevant action outcomes using the next observation:

S¯t\displaystyle\bar{S}_{t} =ℛobs​(St,ot),\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{obs}}(S_{t},o_{t}), (3)
St+1\displaystyle S_{t+1} =ℛeff​(S¯t,ot+1,𝒱t).\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{eff}}(\bar{S}_{t},o_{t+1};\mathcal{V}_{t}).

The first update can establish visible information and object bindings. The second evaluates the set 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} of outcome requirements implicated by the action or an explicit confirmation cue. Using the observation returned by the environment, TAM distinguishes three cases: text entered into a form is a draft, clicking Save is an attempt, and an appropriate confirmation supports a saved result. The accepted result then becomes available to dependent requirements. This keeps progress tied to observed effects while leaving action selection with the base policy.

Retain visual evidence when text is insufficient.

A task-local Evidence Cache ℰ\mathcal{E} stores source images or crops linked to task information and its object bindings. When a requirement needs information whose source screen has left recent context, recalled evidence can restore its value or clarify which object it describes. Recalled images are identified as historical evidence. Current controls and coordinates come from the live screen.

3.3 Advancement as Supervision: Learning Reusable Operations

Advancement supervision learns reusable operations from verified local results, including those within failed workflows. The challenge is both temporal and semantic: identify the productive interaction, then determine what it required and achieved.

Learning from local results.

Each advancement identifies a local result and a candidate segment of preceding interactions. When terminal evaluation nominates an outcome, it enters the same retrospective review. At task termination, an LLM-based reviewer examines the result and recorded actions and observations, including later evidence of confirmation or contradiction. It retains supported operations and selects the steps contributing to their navigation and information acquisition. Review evaluates each operation against the evidence for its local result, including when the larger task fails. TAM separates inputs needed before the retained interaction from information acquired within it. Only the former become the operation’s entry requirements. For example, a route query requires an origin and destination; the driving duration is acquired by the operation itself. This makes the learned query applicable to new routes whose duration the agent still needs to find.

Abstract task values while preserving object identity.

A supported segment yields an Advancement Operator

κ=⟨Rκ,Δκ,Vκ,Bκ,Γκ,𝒜κ⟩.\kappa=\langle R_{\kappa},\Delta_{\kappa},V_{\kappa},B_{\kappa},\Gamma_{\kappa},\mathcal{A}_{\kappa}\rangle. (4)

Its components are entry requirements RκR_{\kappa}, expected advancement Δκ\Delta_{\kappa}, verification condition VκV_{\kappa}, object roles BκB_{\kappa}, optional applicability conditions Γκ\Gamma_{\kappa}, and reviewed GUI realizations 𝒜κ\mathcal{A}_{\kappa}: recorded action sequences together with the interface conditions under which they were observed. Abstraction replaces instance-specific values with roles shared across the inputs, result, and verification target. For example, event details and the creation confirmation must refer to the same event. Concrete GUI entry conditions and action details belong to individual realizations. The persistent Advancement Operator Graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} links each operator to its observed GUI realizations. This lets TAM reuse the same operation while checking each route against the current interface. To consolidate a new sample, TAM compares its input–result relation with the stored operators: compatible samples refine a shared description while retaining distinct GUI realizations. Otherwise, the sample forms a separate operator.

3.4 Operator Reuse: Task Meaning and GUI Realization

An operation can remain useful across changes in its GUI implementation. TAM separates two questions: whether the operation supplies a needed result from available inputs, and whether the current interface supports a recorded route. TAM retrieves operators whose expected results and input roles match a frontier requirement. Among supported candidates, it considers both coverage of remaining requirements and the applicability and reliability of the stored GUI route. Selection retains a bounded set of alternatives across these two criteria, favoring additional requirement coverage. Appendices A.6 and A.10 specify matching, compatibility checks, and selection rules. When the required inputs are available and a stored GUI route passes the interface and reliability checks, the readout includes that route. Otherwise, a supported operator can still supply its required inputs, expected result, and verification cue, with missing inputs explicitly marked. Task knowledge therefore remains useful when a stored route needs adaptation. The actor uses this guidance to choose primitive actions from the current interface. Historical success guides the attempt; current observations determine whether the expected advancement is accepted. If no operator is relevant, ordinary execution continues with the task state and recent context.

4 Experiments

We evaluate task completion on two benchmarks and lifecycle cost on MobileWorld. Component ablations measure the contribution of online state and persistent operators. We also examine whether earlier results remain usable and whether local review produces reliable learning material.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks.

MobileWorld GUI-only tests long-horizon tasks across a broad application suite, including workflows that span multiple apps (Kong et al., 2026). We use the GUI-only interaction setting with standard mobile actions. This setting stresses the preservation of information and results across application boundaries. SPA-Bench English Level 3 evaluates multi-stage workflows within individual smartphone applications at the benchmark’s highest difficulty tier (Chen et al., 2025). Following GUI-explorer, we study the single-app English Level 3 setting with Set-of-Mark (SoM) observations and GPT-4o (Xie et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2024). It complements MobileWorld by testing sustained interaction with real-world applications without requiring cross-app information transfer.

Backbones and memory protocol.

Every MobileWorld method in Table 1 uses Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct and the same limit of 50 controller rounds (Bai et al., 2025). TAM builds persistent memory from interactions in the evaluation task sequence, without a separate application-exploration stage. Task Advancement State and Evidence Cache reset between tasks, reviewed operators remain available to subsequent tasks. Component ablations preserve the base policy, action interface, and interaction budget. On SPA-Bench, we use a task-specific budget of 2​gi+12g_{i}+1 rounds, where gig_{i} is the reference human action count. The official evaluator scores the recorded trajectory after termination; it supplies no intermediate success feedback to the policy. Appendix B.3 specifies execution, memory, and the aggregation protocol.

Metrics.

Success is acceptance by the benchmark’s native evaluator and is reported for both benchmarks. We additionally report the following execution and cost metrics on MobileWorld. Steps averages controller rounds over all runs, including failures, and is interpreted jointly with success. A controller round is one externally counted action decision. Efficiency–Quality Area at 50 rounds (EQA@50) jointly rewards successful completion and fewer controller rounds, assigning zero credit to failures (Wang et al., 2026). Lifecycle Tokens per Solved Task (LTS) divides total model-token expenditure by solved tasks, including memory construction, execution, and failed attempts.

Baselines.

Alongside the memory-free backbone, we compare workflow induction with AWM, tips and shortcuts with Mobile-Agent-E, exploration-built knowledge with GUI-explorer, verified task-state and procedural memory with StructAgent, and proactive context management with MemGUI-Agent (ConAct) (Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025a; Xie et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b). These comparisons cover both state-oriented and experience-oriented approaches. Table 2 combines our SPA-Bench evaluation of TAM and ConAct with published reference results from Xie et al. (2025), retaining the reported observation and backbone for each method.

4.2 Main Results

On MobileWorld, TAM achieves 34.2% success, improving on the strongest evaluated baseline by 5.1 percentage points (Table 1). Relative to the memory-free backbone, the gain is 22.2 points. Across all three app-count groups, TAM outperforms all four compared baselines (Table 3). Its advantage over ConAct is larger on the 62 multi-app tasks, where success reaches 32.3% versus 24.2% (+8.1 points), than on single-app tasks (+1.8 points). The larger multi-app gain supports TAM’s focus on sustaining execution across application boundaries. TAM also attains the highest EQA@50, 29.2%, and uses 20.6 controller rounds on average, showing that the advantage also holds when successful completion is rewarded for taking fewer rounds. TAM uses 0.771M lifecycle tokens per solved task, 38.7% below ConAct’s 1.257M. AWM is slightly cheaper at 0.720M, but completes 13.7% of tasks versus TAM’s 34.2%. TAM offers the strongest completion rate in this comparison at a lifecycle cost close to the cheapest evaluated memory method. This supports the practical value of organizing memory around established task results rather than increasing the interaction budget. On SPA-Bench English Level 3, TAM reaches 57.0% success, 3.3 percentage points above GUI-explorer’s reported 53.7% (Table 2). This is the highest result in the reported comparison. Together, the two benchmarks show that TAM’s benefits occur both in cross-app workflows with an open-source backbone and in difficult single-app tasks with GPT-4o.

4.3 Component Ablations

Table 4 shows that Task Advancement State provides the largest gain, raising success from 12.0% to 28.2%. This gain establishes the value of advancement state for online execution before persistent experience is added. Adding the Advancement Operator Graph to State yields 32.5%, while average steps fall from 23.4 to 20.9. With the Evidence Cache enabled, the Operator Graph adds 5.1 points (29.1% to 34.2%). The Operator Graph improves completion in both cache settings. Online state provides the main gain by making earlier results available to unfinished work, persistent operators add experience about how to obtain the next needed result.

4.4 Mechanism Analysis

Identifying and using task information.

To examine whether acquired information remains usable, we audit archived runs of tasks that require obtaining a value from the environment and using it in a later operation. The comparison covers the same 52 required values across 21 tasks for all five methods. Within each task, identification coverage is the fraction of required values explicitly and correctly stated in online outputs; target-use coverage is the fraction correctly used in their intended fields or objects. Averaging these rates equally across tasks, TAM achieves the highest observed coverage for both identification and target use (Figure 3(a)).

State availability and use.

We use a flat-state control to test the value of relating stored facts to pending requirements. The control retains fact storage and open requirements while removing prerequisite links and their action guidance. To compare the use of available information, we include all target fields in the paired runs whose required source inputs were visible to both agents. The nine eligible fields from five tasks are each assessed under two paired implementation revisions, giving 18 field instances. Over these instances, state availability measures the fraction with the correct value explicitly recorded in the actor’s state. TAM achieves 77.8% versus 55.6% for flat state, while correct target use reaches 77.8% versus 66.7% (Figure 3(b)).

Localizing supervision for operator learning.

For supported advancements written to operator memory, we compare candidate segments with the steps retained after retrospective review. Figure 3(c) shows the 10th–90th percentile profiles, normalized by source-trajectory length. Review reduces the median retained segment length from 20% to 7.7% of the source trajectory. Therefore, the retained supervision is concentrated on local operations rather than the full interaction history.

4.5 Further Analyses

Beyond the main benchmark comparisons, the appendix provides complementary evidence on information retention, state organization, local learning signals, experience reuse, and resource requirements. Appendix D.1 classifies all 117 MobileWorld GUI-only tasks and identifies 52 that require transferring acquired values to later operations, establishing the scope of our field-level diagnostics. Appendix D.2 shows that 95.1% of tracked values remain in state after ten decisions, compared with 57.6% in current XML or recent text, demonstrating sustained access beyond the immediate context. Appendix D.3 finds that TAM assembles all audited inputs before entry in 80% of operations, versus 40% for flat state, when both agents have encountered the required source information. This supports organizing acquired facts around pending operations. In matched tests of access to captured facts, Appendix D.4 reports 96.2% readout accuracy versus 80.8% for ordinary notes at similar input size. TAM also uses 37.3% fewer input tokens per readout than full textual history, combining accurate access with compact context. Appendix D.5 shows that local selection retains 88.3% of correct material versus 64.3% for success-only filtering, with 93.8% correctness among retained values, expanding the pool of reliable learning material. Appendix D.6 shows that 74.8% of audited failed executions containing verified local results contribute retained learning material. Recorded traces connect this material to guidance for later tasks, demonstrating the learning value of partial progress. Appendix D.7 reports 83.3% correctness when binding changed task values and 79.3% correct destination use in the respective field audits, supporting the adaptation of stored experience to new tasks. Finally, Appendix D.8 documents a compact resource footprint across the archived runs, with median shares of 5.7% of actor text for state and guidance and 1.7% of recorded tokens for additional calls.

5 Conclusion

Task Advancement Memory makes established results useful at two timescales. During execution, task reduction supplies acquired information to pending requirements and removes completed requirements. During learning, the interactions yield reusable operations whose entry inputs, outcome, and verification target remain aligned after abstraction. Across MobileWorld and SPA-Bench, TAM improves task completion, with ablations establishing the independent value of Advancement State and further gains from persistent operators. These findings support a task-centered foundation for GUI memory: accumulated progress makes the current problem more concrete, while productive interaction builds capabilities for future workflows.

Limitations

TAM builds task state and reusable operators from observed results. The accuracy of this process depends on model-based interpretation of task requirements and GUI evidence, especially when outcome cues are ambiguous. Improving visual grounding and outcome verification can strengthen both online execution and experience learning.

Our evaluation focuses on MobileWorld GUI-only tasks and the English Level 3 subset of SPA-Bench, covering cross-application workflows and difficult single-application tasks on mobile devices. Extending this evaluation to web and desktop workflows would assess transfer across interface types.

TAM’s persistent operators accumulate across the benchmark task sequences studied here. Longer task streams and repeated application updates introduce further requirements for maintaining relevant experience. The separation between an operation’s intended result and its GUI realizations provides a basis for studying adaptation as interfaces change. Future work can examine operator revision and retirement, together with their effects on retrieval quality and memory-maintenance cost.

Appendix A Method and Implementation Details

This appendix describes how TAM connects the requirements of a task to observed progress and reusable operations. We follow the execution order in Algorithm 1: compile the requirements, maintain task advancement state, retrieve relevant evidence and operators, and review supported local operations for reuse. The same requirement and object identifiers connect these stages.

A.1 Requirements and memory records

A requirement in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} describes either information to acquire or an outcome to achieve. Its record contains a relation name, value type, object roles, prerequisite requirements RqR_{q}, and a verification condition VqV_{q}. Structured values also specify their required fields. An optional condition γq\gamma_{q} identifies the branch in which the requirement applies. For example, an event record can contain its title, date, and time, while a notification requirement depends on that record and the recipient’s contact information. Dependencies describe the information consumed by an operation; the GUI route is chosen during execution.

The state StS_{t} associates each requirement with its status, current bindings, and evidence references, as described in Section 3.1. Bindings preserve the relation between a value and its object: an event time belongs to the specified event, and an address belongs to the specified recipient. Evidence references identify the observation step and saved source artifact. The implementation also records artifact digests so that a reused image retains its original identity.

The Evidence Cache ℰ\mathcal{E} stores visual support for task-local facts. The persistent graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} stores operators and their GUI realizations. An operator records its entry inputs, expected advancement, verification condition, object roles, and applicability conditions. Its realizations retain the corresponding action sequences and interface contexts. This separates the result an operation provides from the route used to obtain it. Task state and cached evidence reset at the task boundary; reviewed operators remain available to subsequent tasks.

A.2 Compiling the task requirements

At task start, the LLM-based compiler receives the natural-language instruction and proposes information and outcome requirements in JSON. It assigns types, names the necessary fields, and specifies which requirements supply inputs to each outcome. For a conditional request, it also represents the condition and its dependent requirement. Compilation operates on the instruction; it does not require advance access to the applications or their task-specific contents.

The implementation combines the proposal with schema normalization. This resolves requirement references, checks field types, and preserves prerequisite relations when bounding the graph size. The default target is 12 requirements; dependencies needed by a retained requirement are preserved. Explicit instruction values, such as a requested recipient, subject, or message, are kept as constraints on the corresponding outcome. They specify what the agent must achieve and are kept separate from observations of what it has achieved.

Consider the request to read an event’s details and notify a contact. The compiler separates the event information, the contact endpoint, and the notification outcome. If the task also asks for an independent numerical answer, that calculation is connected only to the outputs that use it. The resulting graph therefore preserves independent branches of the request instead of requiring every intermediate result before any outcome can be pursued.

A.3 Updating and reading task advancement state

The actor reports task-relevant observations alongside its action. Each observation update identifies a requirement, a value or structured fields, and the evidence that supports it. The update format distinguishes source information, derived values, visible drafts, collection coverage, and observed effects. These roles retain the difference between reading an event’s time, entering that time into a form, and observing a saved event. The runtime associates the proposed update with its requirement and source observation, checks the field structure, and updates the corresponding binding. Model-based extraction interprets the observed content; reference and schema checks preserve its association with the task and artifact.

Source information can be established from the current observation. Relevant outcomes are assessed from the observation returned after an action, using the requirement’s verification condition. For instance, text visible in a message composer describes a draft; the sent-message view provides evidence about the resulting message. Both the content and its recipient matter when the task specifies them. The two updates in Eq. 3 thus use the observations already produced by the interaction loop.

Structured requirements retain missing fields until they are supplied. Collections preserve observed members separately from evidence that the requested scope has been covered. Similarly, an absence claim refers to a particular source and search scope. Contradictory observations leave the affected requirement conflicted until further evidence resolves it. This keeps later inputs tied to the information that has been established.

Presenting the remaining work.

The actor receives the established bindings and a requirement readout that distinguishes available inputs from missing inputs. An input shared by several requirements is referenced from the same state record. This is the implementation of the residual-task representation described in Section 3.2: completed requirements no longer constitute pending work, while their values remain available to their consumers. The frontier FtF_{t} identifies unresolved requirements whose dependencies and branch conditions are satisfied.

In the event example, reading the event details supplies the notification’s content. After the contact endpoint is established, the notification has its required inputs. The actor can proceed using those values even after leaving the source applications. The readout organizes the next decision; it does not issue an action or replace the original task instruction. TAM’s full-method configuration leaves primitive action selection to the base policy.

A.4 Recalling visual evidence

A cache entry links a saved screenshot or crop to the accepted relation, object binding, and source step. The cache is queried when a current requirement needs information whose source is no longer represented in the actor’s recent visual context. Selection follows the requirement’s input dependencies and matches the corresponding bindings. If several facts come from the same image, that image is attached once.

The implementation forms a packet covering the required source evidence within a limit of three recalled images. Evidence already present in the actor context contributes to that coverage. Each recalled image is marked as a past observation and supplied with a reference identifier. When the actor reads a value from it, the observation update cites that identifier. The resulting value follows the ordinary state-update path. Current control locations and coordinates are grounded in the live observation.

Cache selection does not invoke another model. The selected images enter the ordinary actor call, where their visual tokens are included in the cost. If no matching packet is available, execution proceeds with the current observation, recent history, and task state.

A.5 Reviewing local operations and abstracting their inputs

An accepted advancement records the affected requirement, its bindings, supporting evidence, and the preceding interaction segment. This initial segment retains context before the use of relevant inputs. It is a candidate for review: some of its interactions may be navigation, repeated attempts, or work unrelated to the established result.

At task end, the reviewer receives the candidates, their recorded actions, the result observations, and available later evidence. It decides whether each local result is supported, selects the steps to retain, and cites the supporting artifacts. Later observations can confirm the result or reveal a reversal or object mismatch. Terminal success can nominate an outcome candidate for review, it does not replace the local evidence judgment. The independent outcome-quality audit excludes such evaluator-nominated candidates (Appendix D.5). Correctly reading an event remains a useful operation when a later notification fails; a successful task can likewise contain unproductive attempts that need not enter its reusable operation.

Identifying the entry inputs.

TAM saves the accepted task facts available before each step. Once the reviewer selects a segment, the snapshot at its retained start identifies which inputs were already available. Changes within the segment identify information acquired by the operation itself. This distinction determines RκR_{\kappa}: a value first obtained inside the retained segment is an internal result, rather than an input required before the operation starts. If review chooses a later start, the corresponding later snapshot supplies its entry state. The implementation preserves the navigation and information-acquisition steps needed to support the selected local result.

For example, a segment that opens a calendar and reads an event can learn an operation for acquiring event details. A subsequent segment that starts with those details and sends a notification can learn an operation that consumes them. The second operation’s inputs should not be assigned to the first merely because both appear in the same completed workflow. Conversely, reviewing a segment from a later starting point must use the information available at that point, rather than the task’s final state.

Consolidating an operation.

For a supported segment, the reviewer provides a short description of the entry inputs, local result, and reusable method. It replaces task-specific values with object roles and compares the input–result relation with nearby stored operators. Compatible samples refine one operator while preserving their individual GUI realizations. Materially different inputs or outcomes produce separate operators. Different names, dates, or layouts alone do not require a separate semantic operation.

For the route query in Figure 2, the entry snapshot contains Orlando and Miami as the origin and destination. The driving duration is absent at entry and is obtained from the route-result screen. Abstraction replaces the two locations with origin and destination roles. The operator requires those roles, returns their driving duration, and checks that the displayed route uses the requested transportation type. Its recorded realization is Maps →\rightarrow route query →\rightarrow route result. The duration remains the result to obtain in a new task, rather than a prerequisite copied from the completed source trajectory.

The stored record links this description to the retained steps and evidence. The expected result and verification condition refer to the same object roles as the inputs. The graph can therefore preserve an operation such as creating an event from given details while retaining different observed routes through the calendar interface. New evidence refines the shared description while preserving each observed route.

A.6 Retrieval and actor readout

Retrieval begins with the remaining requirements and their available inputs. TAM compares candidate operators with the needed result and checks whether their input roles and applicability conditions fit the current task. It then assesses each stored realization against the current application and interface context. These are the task-relevance and GUI-compatibility questions introduced in Section 3.4.

The readout includes the operation’s required inputs, expected advancement, and verification cue. When a realization fits the live interface, it also includes the corresponding route. Otherwise, the semantic operation still describes a useful result and how to recognize it, while the actor chooses a route from the current screen. Candidate selection retains a bounded set of relevant operations and avoids filling the context with equivalent routes. The retrieved-memory budget applies to this operator readout; task state and recent observations have their own context limits.

Applying an operator uses the current task’s bindings. Historical task values remain part of the source record, while the actor grounds the present action on the live interface. The expected advancement becomes an established requirement only when current observations support it. The same state-update process therefore connects learning from one task with verification in the next.

A.7 Model interfaces and call accounting

Table 5 summarizes the inputs and outputs of the implementation’s model calls. Requirements, observation references, and retained step identifiers provide the common structure across calls. The actor also maintains a concise execution summary containing findings, attempted routes, and remaining work alongside the structured task state.

Task compilation occurs at initialization, acting follows the environment’s decision loop, and retrospective review occurs after termination. The cache and the organization of available and missing inputs introduce no separate model calls. Model-cost accounting includes compilation, acting, triggered extraction, format repair, and retrospective review, together with the input tokens of recalled images. The benchmark settings and context budgets are reported in Appendix B; Appendix D.8 analyzes the observed allocation of inference and actor context.

A.8 Structured interfaces and representative prompts

The compiler returns a JSON object with a goal_slots list. Each requirement has a stable schema name and a goal_kind: resource denotes information to obtain, and done denotes an observable GUI effect. The optional type and required_fields specify its value structure; requires names prerequisite requirements. consumption_role distinguishes a target endpoint, rendered content, decision input, lookup key, attachment, or verification target. entity_pattern and retrieval_cues describe the object and where to seek it. A conditional requirement names its branch_predicate; alternative decision requirements can also name one another through alternative_to and specify condition_polarity. effect_constraints preserves the task’s required recipient, content, attachments, and fields to be checked at completion.

For example, the compiler prompt contains the following complete small output example. The date requirement provides content to the message effect; a concrete task can add its recipient and other required inputs.

{"goal_slots": [
  {"schema": "arrival_date",
   "goal_kind": "resource",
   "type": "date"},
  {"schema": "sms_sent",
   "goal_kind": "done",
   "type": "done",
   "requires": ["arrival_date"],
   "effect_constraints": {
     "expected_render_schemas":
       ["arrival_date"]}}
]}

A stored binding records schema, type, value_norm, and state; entity_key identifies its object, while evidence_ref and source_step_id retain the supporting artifact and source step.

Each update names an op, the displayed schema, a scalar value or structured fields, an evidence_role, and a short evidence_text. The roles are source, derived, draft, coverage, and effect. A recalled-image update additionally cites the displayed reference_evidence_id. These are proposals: the runtime associates them with the task requirement and recorded observation. An outcome-extraction call returns an observations list with schema, evidence_ref, evidence, and fields. Its parser admits only listed requirement names, the current post-action reference, and a nonempty visible witness.

The following excerpts are taken verbatim from the prompts used in our implementation; the task-specific JSON packet and images follow the instructions.

Task compilation.

“Infer the smallest set of goal slots required to determine task completion.” “Use requires only for other goal-slot schemas that are semantic prerequisites for this claim; do not include app names, actions, or concrete values.”

Outcome extraction.

“Report only the listed outcomes whose verification conditions are visibly satisfied for the correct object and values. A draft, an attempt, or disappearance of a form alone is not confirmation.” “Use observations: [] when nothing is confirmed.”

Retrospective review and abstraction.

“Task success is not a local-evidence label. Keep supplied anchor/effect/step/evidence IDs.” “Use inputs available at the retained start. Information acquired inside the trace is internal work, not a prerequisite.” “Compare that local input-to-outcome relation with nearby_operators.” “Use task roles, not instance values. The host retains each real route; do not average routes.”

The reviewer returns one decision per candidate, containing its anchor_id, effect_schema, source_validity (supported, ambiguous, or contradicted), retained_step_ids, cited_evidence_ids, and rationale. For a supported result, an optional operator_update contains same_operator_id and short descriptions of its inputs, outcome, and method.

A.9 Candidate boundaries and retained interactions

An accepted local result supplies the candidate endpoint ee. For resource alignment, the implementation ranks recorded transitions up to the detected endpoint by Hi=4​xi+3​ni+2​max⁡(0,zi−yi)H_{i}=4x_{i}+3n_{i}+2\max(0,z_{i}-y_{i}). Here xi,yi,zix_{i},y_{i},z_{i} are the fractions of claim tokens appearing in the action target, pre-action UI, and post-action UI, respectively; nin_{i} is the fraction newly visible after the action. Claim tokens come from the proposed values, fields, and evidence text, with generic stop words removed. The highest-scoring transition is used, with later steps breaking ties, only if Hi≥0.35H_{i}\geq 0.35; backdating additionally requires an exact claimed value in that transition’s visible post-action UI. Otherwise the detected endpoint is retained. Let rr be the earliest recorded availability step, before ee, among the candidate’s required inputs, and let pp be the previous captured advancement step strictly before ee. If a backdated endpoint is at or before the most recent advancement, that advancement does not constrain the start. The initial start is max⁡(r,p+1)\max(r,p+1) when both exist, rr or p+1p+1 when only one exists, and the episode start otherwise. The candidate contains the bounded suffix of this interval through ee; the default setting retains at most eight steps. An empty recorded slice falls back to the detected transition as a single-step candidate. Thus the reviewer receives a local candidate rather than choosing an unrestricted interval from the full episode.

The reviewer chooses a nonempty subset of supplied step identifiers that includes ee, and cites evidence identifiers from the supplied packet. The host validates both sets. It then closes the selection over observed input support: input-entry steps not marked as making no progress, or selections of a result or recipient bound to a required input, identify the earliest supporting step. The retained route includes the nonempty, non-wait actions from there through ee. For acquisition without entry inputs, it also retains the navigation/read prefix from the latest recorded app opening, or the bounded prefix if no app opening is present. If required inputs have no identified support step, the validated reviewer selection is retained.

Entry inputs are determined after this closure. The snapshot immediately before the retained start supplies the available facts; subsequent snapshots through the endpoint identify acquired or updated facts. An input requirement is removed only if it was first acquired inside the retained interaction and was absent at entry. A later retained start therefore uses its own earlier-state snapshot. Missing history remains unknown. When its application and activity are recorded, the GUI realization’s entry condition is taken from the first retained step’s observed pre-state; otherwise the original entry scope is retained.

A.10 Operator identity, matching, and GUI readout

Retrieval compares operators learned from reviewed interactions with requirements compiled from the current instruction. It checks the required result and input roles before considering a recorded GUI route. Our MobileWorld and SPA-Bench configurations share the reference settings specified below. Task bindings and GUI context are recomputed for each retrieval; execution evidence updates the reliability of each operation and route.

The stored semantic record names its operator_kind and operator_family, entry requires, expected effects, and verifies. Its input profiles bind requirement schemas to parameter roles; guard variants preserve optional conditions. The verification_contract names the result schema, the required result fields, and the evidence relation. Separate GUI records link to this semantic identifier and retain the entry context, typed route, retained source steps, required/capability roles, and evidence provenance.

Consolidation.

The reviewer compares the retained operation’s input-to-result relation with the supplied nearby operators. It proposes an existing identifier only when that relation is compatible; otherwise it returns null. The host accepts a proposed merge only if the identifier occurs among the supplied operators, the description is nonempty, and the result’s canonical family matches. Otherwise it stores the supported sample separately. A merge updates the description and retains observed input profiles, guards, and individual GUI realizations. The host does not average their action sequences.

Schema canonicalization.

Compiler names are lowercased and normalized with underscores. Marker-based alias maps assign canonical result families and input roles. Effect families encode domain and operation; resource families retain recognized role/domain and positional qualifiers. Thus SMS-Sent and text_message_sent map to text_send, while meeting_time and event_time map to resource:event_time. Input profiles additionally normalize declared roles, such as render to content. Unrecognized effects use predicate:<schema>; resources lacking a recognized role retain resource:<schema>. In fallback schema comparison, qualifier conflicts mean opposing marker groups (e.g., start/end, source/destination, departure/arrival) or aggregate versus nonaggregate markers; these receive zero similarity.

Semantic matching.

Semantic matching tests whether an operator can supply the result of a pending requirement. Result types and input roles constrain eligibility; normalized schema comparison supports records with incomplete type metadata. An explicitly typed source must match the target’s resource-acquisition or effect-realization kind and canonical result family. For records without an explicit family, TAM first derives a canonical family from the schema name. Agreement with the target family gives a match score of 11. Otherwise, normalized schema comparison checks exact identity, qualifier conflicts, effect-family or resource-role agreement, and finally substring or token overlap. The corresponding reference scores are 11 for exact identity, 00 for qualifier conflicts, 0.940.94 for a shared effect family, 0.860.86 for a shared resource role, 0.820.82 for a substring match, and token Jaccard otherwise. The reference fallback threshold is τm,0=0.80\tau_{m,0}=0.80. Incompatible effect families and effect–resource pairs are capped at 0.590.59 and excluded from feedback-calibrated matching, so name overlap cannot override a type conflict. Compatible input profiles must agree on whether the operation consumes inputs. When both profiles have role metadata, the source profile must cover the target’s required roles. The matched operation is rebound to the current requirement and its inputs. Reuse preserves the input–result relation while substituting the new task values; historical values remain provenance. Profiles lacking role metadata retain the coarser check on whether inputs are consumed.

GUI compatibility and reliability.

GUI compatibility tests a recorded route against the live interface. Each realization retains its own entry conditions, so a shared semantic operation can support different interface-specific routes. A route needs a supported semantic source, an eligible stored lifecycle, a valid typed route identity, available target inputs, and the capability roles required by those inputs. Typed actions must specify meaningful roles: typing requires both target and value roles, opening an app a value role, and clicking a target role. Known application or page-role conflicts reject a route. An activity conflict also rejects it unless the page role agrees. Otherwise applicability uses application/activity agreement and token overlap with the entry context; matching layout fingerprints provide additional support.

The GUI context records the application, activity, page role, and a layout fingerprint. The fingerprint hashes the UI tree after masking displayed text, content descriptions, and digits; without a UI tree, it hashes the application, activity, and orientation. The first 16 hexadecimal characters of SHA-256 identify the normalized layout. After the conflict checks, the reference implementation scores the available entry-context evidence:

a=min⁡(amax,b+wJ​J+wA​ACLOSEOPEN+wV​V+wh​h).\begin{split}a=\min\bigl(a_{\max},\;b+w_{J}J+w_{A}A\\ \qquad\qquad+w_{V}V+w_{h}h\bigr).\end{split}

Here JJ is token Jaccard between live and stored entry descriptions; A,V∈{0,1}A,V\in\{0,1\} indicate application and activity compatibility; and hh counts matching known page-role and layout features. The reference settings use b=0.08b=0.08, (wJ,wA,wV,wh)=(0.42,0.28,0.18,0.08)(w_{J},w_{A},w_{V},w_{h})=(0.42,0.28,0.18,0.08), and amax=0.72a_{\max}=0.72. Application and activity compatibility test normalized name equality or containment, followed by overlap or shared prefixes among informative name tokens. Missing both an informative entry description and an application pair gives a=0a=0.

TAM maintains semantic and route reliability separately. Reuse trials are assessed during execution, and reviewed outcomes update persistent counts at task end. An observed target advancement supports the semantic operation, including when the actor adapts its actions. Route success additionally requires following and completing the stored route and reaching its destination. Reviewed counterexamples update the corresponding semantic or route failure count. Ambiguous or unattributed outcomes are censored; repeated observation identifiers are counted once. For count-backed records, both estimates use additive smoothing:

rj=sj+αjsj+fj+αj+βj,j∈{sem,gui}.r_{j}=\frac{s_{j}+\alpha_{j}}{s_{j}+f_{j}+\alpha_{j}+\beta_{j}},\quad j\in\{\mathrm{sem},\mathrm{gui}\}.

Here sj,fjs_{j},f_{j} are the corresponding positive and negative evidence counts. The constants αj,βj\alpha_{j},\beta_{j} are smoothing pseudocounts that stabilize estimates from sparse observations. Their reference values are (αsem,βsem)=(2,1)(\alpha_{\rm sem},\beta_{\rm sem})=(2,1) and (αgui,βgui)=(1,1)(\alpha_{\rm gui},\beta_{\rm gui})=(1,1).

A semantic source must pass its reliability gate. Recorded-route guidance additionally requires sufficient route reliability and GUI applicability, together with the compatibility checks above. The reference thresholds are τsem,0=0.55\tau_{{\rm sem},0}=0.55, τgui,0=0.45\tau_{{\rm gui},0}=0.45, and τa,0=0.38\tau_{a,0}=0.38. As observations accumulate, changes in reliability can enable or suppress route guidance. This adapts reuse to experience with each stored operation and route.

For feedback-calibrated retrieval, the four admission thresholds use the reviewed local reuse outcomes accumulated within the same memory sequence. Between tasks, each threshold is set to the midpoint of the positive and negative mean pre-execution scores, with its reference value contributing one fixed pseudo-observation to each mean. Semantic outcomes calibrate the matching and semantic gates; outcomes of attempted routes calibrate the route and applicability gates. The reference value is used when either outcome class is absent or the positive mean is not higher. Type, input-role, and interface conflicts remain hard rejections.

If no route passes, a supported semantic operation can still provide its inputs, result, and verification cue, with missing inputs marked explicitly. This preserves task-level guidance when a recorded GUI implementation is unsuitable. Scoped negative evidence remains a rejection in either mode.

Eligible alternatives undergo two-axis ϵ\epsilon-Pareto selection, followed by a bound that first favors new requirement coverage and then distinct route families. For persistent graph retrieval, the two axes measure requirement coverage and execution support:

C\displaystyle C =λ∑q∈Utmq𝟏[mq≥τC],\displaystyle=\lambda\sum_{q\in U_{t}}m_{q}\mathbf{1}[m_{q}\geq\tau_{C}],
E\displaystyle E =η​a+(1−η)​rgui.\displaystyle=\eta a+(1-\eta)r_{\rm gui}.

Here UtU_{t} contains the remaining requirements, and mqm_{q} is the largest schema-match score between qq and the candidate’s target-bound results. The reference settings use λ=1.25\lambda=1.25, τC=0.66\tau_{C}=0.66, η=0.62\eta=0.62, and ϵ=0.05\epsilon=0.05, retaining at most two alternatives. The result and verification sets coincide on this path. Semantic-only advice has E=0E=0; a persistent candidate without typed requirement coverage is rejected. A candidate is removed when another is at least as good minus ϵ\epsilon on both axes and better by more than ϵ\epsilon on either.

Conflicting upstream evidence.

The readout excludes unresolved or conflicted facts from available inputs, so dependent requirements identify those inputs as missing. In the typed state kernel, a pending effect whose inputs cease to be established becomes unprepared; an attempted effect with a newly conflicted input becomes ambiguous and calls for further evidence. A separately confirmed effect retains its own observation-backed status when an upstream input becomes conflicted.

A.11 A complete illustrative operator for Figure 2

The following instantiates every component of the route-query operator in Figure 2. Its role names and route description are schematic, not an additional measured trajectory. Let oo and dd denote the origin and destination and τ\tau the observed driving duration.

Entry requirements RκR_{\kappa}.

Origin and destination are available as the two route endpoints. The driving duration is not an entry input.

Expected advancement Δκ\Delta_{\kappa}.

Acquire driving​_​duration​(o,d)=τ\mathrm{driving\_duration}(o,d)=\tau for the specified route.

A route-result observation shows driving mode, the bound origin and destination, and the reported duration for that route.
