These later results are outside the route-query operator. On reuse, new endpoints replace o,do,d, and a new observation must establish the new duration before it enters task state.

Appendix B Experimental Setup

B.1 Benchmarks and Observations

MobileWorld.

We evaluate the GUI-only partition of MobileWorld (Kong et al., 2026). Based on the released task metadata (Tongyi-MAI, 2025), this partition contains 117 tasks across 15 GUI applications, with 105 English and 12 Chinese instructions. The application counts in the task metadata divide these tasks into 55 single-app, 48 two-app, and 14 three-app workflows. Tasks include communication, scheduling, document handling, file management, and shopping. The GUI-only setting uses touch, text entry, scrolling, navigation, application launch, waiting, and termination. It excludes MCP tools and simulated-user clarification.

The observation interface supplies the current screenshot and the available Android UI tree. Each method constructs its own history and memory context from these observations. MobileWorld initializes the device and application data for each task. Its native evaluators check the requested result through task-specific answer checks, backend state, device-local files, or application callbacks. Evaluation data are kept separate from actor observations.

SPA-Bench.

We use the English single-app Level 3 setting of SPA-Bench (Chen et al., 2025). Based on the released task metadata (AI Agents 2030, 2024), this split contains 50 tasks across 36 applications, with reference human trajectories comprising 9–18 annotated actions. These multi-stage single-app workflows complement the cross-app demands of MobileWorld. The split is identified by the English single-app task file and its Level 3 difficulty annotations; task instructions are used as released. As specified in Section 4.1, TAM uses GPT-4o with Set-of-Mark observations. Appendix B.3 describes initialization, action execution, final evaluation, and memory continuity for this setting.

B.2 MobileWorld Implementation and Evaluation

Interaction budget.

All MobileWorld methods use Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct and a budget of 50 controller rounds. A round is an externally counted action decision, including a wait or context-management action. Some baseline decisions expand into several primitive actions; these actions are recorded separately while the decision contributes one controller round. Internal memory operations that make no environment action do not consume a round. Their model calls contribute to token expenditure.

All MobileWorld methods follow the same evaluation and stopping protocol. The native evaluator checks the task after each executed GUI action, and execution stops immediately when it confirms success. For decisions containing multiple primitive actions, this check occurs after each primitive action. Otherwise, execution ends when the agent terminates or reaches the 50-round budget, and the final state is evaluated. Any terminal answer is submitted before evaluation. The evaluator’s reference answers and internal state are not supplied to the actor. SPA-Bench uses its own task-specific budget and post-execution evaluation procedure, detailed in Appendix B.3.

Model and context settings.

TAM uses temperature zero. Table 6 records the reference implementation’s actor settings for both benchmarks. The actor receives the live screenshot, task state, and recent action history. The Evidence Cache can additionally supply the source images selected for a current requirement, as described in Appendix A.4. Task compilation and operator review use the model interfaces summarized in Appendix A.7.

Persistent memory.

The following memory lifecycle applies to both benchmarks. TAM builds its operator library from the task sequence without a separate application-exploration stage. Task Advancement State and the Evidence Cache are cleared at every task boundary. Reviewed operators persist within the evaluation sequence and become available after the source task ends. Thus a task uses the library available at its start; its own retrospective review contributes to later tasks. The task manifest fixes the sequence, and the library is maintained across execution batches. Memory stores are separate for different methods and ablation configurations. Methods with a preconstructed knowledge bank load that bank before execution and retain their own retrieval mechanism.

Task outcomes and retries.

Native evaluation determines task success: MobileWorld uses the per-action and final checks described above, whereas SPA-Bench scores the recorded trajectory after execution. A transport retry resends the model request within the same decision and does not add a GUI action. Interrupted attempts caused by unavailable services or an invalid environment initialization are retained separately from completed task outcomes. A task is retried only when its initial conditions and memory boundary can be restored without duplicating side effects or committed memory. The experiment ledger preserves the original attempt, reported model usage, and reason for retry. Ordinary task failures are not rerun to select a better outcome.

B.3 SPA-Bench Implementation and Evaluation

Environment and action interface.

SPA-Bench tasks run in an Android emulator controlled through Android Debug Bridge (ADB). Before each task, the adapter restores the device snapshot, performs the benchmark’s task initialization, and captures a fresh observation of the target application. Device and capture-service preparation occurs before policy execution. Snapshot restoration resets device-local state, external account state is a separate task prerequisite. The adapter supports touch, long press, dragging, text entry, scrolling, navigation, application launch, waiting, and termination. These operations act on the live interface. The actor receives the released instruction, current SoM observation, and its method’s history and memory, without access to reference trajectories or evaluator key components.

Interaction budget and stopping.

Following the released runner’s default convention (AI Agents 2030, 2024), task ii has a budget of Bi=2​gi+1B_{i}=2g_{i}+1 rounds, where gig_{i} is its annotated human action count. Our controller reserves the final round for termination, allowing at most 2​gi2g_{i} GUI interactions. Waiting and context-management decisions that issue an environment action consume a round; internal memory computations and request retries do not create additional GUI interactions. Execution ends when the policy terminates or the budget is exhausted. An agent’s completion declaration closes the trajectory but does not establish benchmark success.

Official evaluation.

We use SPA-Bench’s single-app evaluator with its result_only reasoning mode and with_action trajectory representation (AI Agents 2030, 2024). The evaluator first searches the recorded screenshots for the task’s textual key components using OCR. If this screening stage passes, GPT-4o assesses the instruction and screenshot trajectory with action annotations. The resulting official success decision determines the binary task outcome. Evaluation is performed after execution rather than after each action, and its annotations and judgments are not fed back into online action selection.

Memory across tasks.

The persistent-memory protocol in Appendix B.2 also applies to SPA-Bench: TAM begins with an empty operator library and retains reviewed operators in task order across execution batches. Learning uses observed local results and retrospective review, without using official evaluator annotations as memory content. For the SPA-Bench ConAct baseline, we carry its model-maintained explicit UI-memory dictionary across tasks as a declared lifecycle extension to the released controller. Native memory add, update, and delete operations are preserved, while folded action history and step indices reset for each task. This extension adds no separate summarization, retrieval, or learning call. Each method maintains its own store over the declared sequence.

Comparison protocol.

Our TAM and ConAct evaluations use the same GPT-4o backbone, task instructions, observation interface, initialization procedure, and task-specific interaction budgets. Each method retains its own memory representation and context management. Table 2 also includes the first seven baselines and GUI-explorer as published reference results from Xie et al. (2025). Their reported inputs and backbones are retained; the shared execution protocol applies to our implementations rather than retroactively to those published runs. The MobileWorld baseline adaptations in Appendix C concern Table 1.

Evaluation sequences and aggregation.

The design uses all 50 official English single-app Level 3 tasks in two complete evaluation sequences. Each task receives one scored attempt per sequence. TAM and ConAct share the task orders, generated from the lexicographically sorted task identifiers with order seeds 0 and 1. These seeds determine task order, they do not control model sampling. Each method starts each sequence with an empty persistent store. Task-local state and the environment reset between tasks, while persistent memory accumulates within the sequence. For method mm, let ym​r​i∈{0,1}y_{mri}\in\{0,1\} be the official outcome for task ii in sequence rr. The reporting rule is

Sm​r\displaystyle S_{mr} =10050​∑i=150ym​r​i,\displaystyle=\frac{100}{50}\sum_{i=1}^{50}y_{mri}, (5)
S¯m\displaystyle\bar{S}_{m} =12​∑r=12Sm​r,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{r=1}^{2}S_{mr},
sm\displaystyle s_{m} =12​∑r=12(Sm​r−S¯m)2.\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\sum_{r=1}^{2}(S_{mr}-\bar{S}_{m})^{2}}.

Each of TAM and ConAct contributes 100 scored task episodes (50 tasks in each of two complete sequences), giving 200 scored episodes across the two methods. All tasks have equal weight, and percentages are rounded only after aggregation. Variation across the two sequences describes the combined effects of task order and execution variability.

Memory updates and interrupted attempts.

Under this design, task-end learning runs after every valid episode, including failures, using the review and storage rules in Section 3.3. The terminal binary verdict can participate in the disclosed task-end review, hidden reference answers and evaluator annotations are not stored as task knowledge. Operators become available after the source task ends. Task failures, premature termination, and exhausted action budgets count as zero and retain their place in the sequence. Only external infrastructure faults that prevent valid execution or scoring permit a replacement attempt. If that state cannot be restored, the sequence restarts from empty memory in the same order. Persistent infrastructure failure is reported as an incomplete sequence rather than a reduced task denominator.

B.4 Component Ablations

The component study in Table 4 varies the enabled memory components while retaining the base policy, decoding settings, observation adapter, action interface, recent-history window, and interaction budget. All configurations with Task Advancement State use the same task compiler and state-update procedure. Table 7 specifies the interventions.

Disabling the Evidence Cache removes recalled source images while retaining established bindings and ordinary history. Disabling the Advancement Operator Graph removes persistent retrieval and task-end operator learning while retaining online state updates. Each configuration maintains a separate library over the same task sequence. The flat-state comparison in Appendix D.3 is a separate intervention on the organization of task-local information.

B.5 Metric Definitions

Let NN be the number of evaluated task instances, si∈{0,1}s_{i}\in\{0,1\} the native-evaluator outcome, and aia_{i} the number of controller rounds up to the stopping point. Under the common MobileWorld protocol, a successful trajectory ends at the first evaluator-confirmed success; an unsuccessful trajectory ends at agent termination or the round budget. We report

Success\displaystyle\mathrm{Success} =100N​∑i=1Nsi,\displaystyle=\frac{100}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}s_{i}, (6)
Steps\displaystyle\mathrm{Steps} =1N​∑i=1Nai.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}.

Steps includes both successful and unsuccessful tasks and is read alongside Success.

Efficiency–Quality Area.

Following the fixed-budget formulation of MMBench-GUI (Wang et al., 2026), we compute

EQA​@​B=100N​∑i=1Nsi​max⁡(0,1−aiB),\mathrm{EQA@}B=\frac{100}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}s_{i}\max\!\left(0,1-\frac{a_{i}}{B}\right), (7)

with B=50B=50 for MobileWorld. EQA@50 uses the same stopping point as Steps. Each successful trajectory contributes according to its completion length; a failed trajectory contributes zero. EQA@50 therefore rewards success achieved with fewer decisions.

Lifecycle Tokens per Solved Task.

Let TbuildT_{\mathrm{build}} be the model-token expenditure for constructing memory before evaluation, and TonlineT_{\mathrm{online}} the expenditure during the task sequence, including actor, state-update, retrieval, reflection, review, and repair calls. Then

LTS=Tbuild+Tonline∑isi.\mathrm{LTS}=\frac{T_{\mathrm{build}}+T_{\mathrm{online}}}{\sum_{i}s_{i}}. (8)

The numerator includes input and output tokens from successful and failed attempts. Execution calls are counted through the stopping point. Subsequent task-end reflection, review, and memory updates are also included. Vision and cached-input tokens follow the provider’s reported usage. Construction shared across tasks is counted once in the numerator and amortized over the solved tasks. We report LTS in millions of tokens. As indicated in Table 1, StructAgent and GUI-explorer have lower-bound LTS values because the available ledgers exclude their original knowledge-bank construction.

The mechanism analyses use the task, field, operation, or episode units defined in the Analysis Protocols and Sample Definitions in Appendix D. Those diagnostic populations are separate from the benchmark-level denominators above.

Appendix C Baseline Adaptations

All MobileWorld methods use the evaluation and stopping protocol in Appendix B.2. The integrations retain each method’s memory representation, update procedure, and internal model roles. Adapters translate their actions to the common mobile interface and expose the current screenshot, available UI-tree information, and application-launch operation. Internal calls contribute to the lifecycle accounting in Appendix B.5.

AWM (Wang et al., 2025b).

AWM induces workflow descriptions from successful trajectories and replaces task-specific arguments with variables. The online adapter updates the workflow library at task boundaries and includes its text in the actor prompt in source order, up to 12,000 characters. Induction requires at least two actionable steps and has a 2,048-token output limit. The actor retains the task’s previous action history and uses a 1,024-token output limit. Workflow descriptions preserve application and affordance names while abstracting instance values and omitting absolute coordinates.

Mobile-Agent-E (Wang et al., 2025a).

The integration retains the Manager, Operator, Action Reflector, Notetaker, and the experience reflectors for tips and shortcuts. Its perception pipeline combines OCR and icon descriptions with available UI-tree controls. After an action, the agent observes the result, reflects on the action, and updates its notes. In the evolution setting, tips and shortcuts persist across tasks, while working notes reset. The optional experience selector is disabled, so available tips and shortcuts are supplied directly. Role responses have a 2,048-token limit. Shortcut expansion is preserved, with its atomic actions logged separately from the controller decision.

StructAgent (Wu et al., 2026).

The adapter retains structured task state, planning, perception, milestone verification, completion auditing, and recovery. It uses the released fixed experience bank with up to ten retrieved items and at most five planner images. The action adapter translates supported operations to Android interactions; desktop shell, browser-control, and office tools are unavailable in the GUI-only environment. The default role output limit is 1,500 tokens, with role-specific requests capped at 8,192. The original experience bank remains fixed during the task sequence.

GUI-explorer (Xie et al., 2025).

The adapter preserves exploration-derived knowledge, multimodal retrieval, model-based ranking, action selection, and step summarization. The live screen queries the knowledge base through its embedding and FAISS pipeline. Retrieval requests one candidate per image query at a similarity threshold of 0.9. The ranker selects knowledge relevant to the current instruction, and step summaries retain execution history. Action selection and summarization use a 1,000-token response limit. The Device interface maps selected actions to MobileWorld while retaining this retrieval and execution loop.

MemGUI-Agent (ConAct) (Liu et al., 2026b).

We adapt the MemGUI-Agent implementation released with MobileWorld. It retains the five-part tagged response format, structured context, history folding, and explicit context-management operations. The actor receives one current screenshot with the shared UI-tree and application-launch extensions; its own context operations manage earlier information. A context-management operation executes a wait and consumes one controller round. Context resets at each task boundary. The response limit is 8,192 tokens to accommodate the tagged sections and rewritten context. Parsing permits up to three attempts on unchanged messages; these attempts are distinct from transport retries and do not introduce extra environment actions.

Appendix D Additional Results and Analysis

The following analyses examine information retention, input preparation, operator learning and reuse, and resource allocation. They draw on benchmark metadata, historical execution archives, paired state controls, and readout tests at fixed checkpoints. The benchmark comparisons measure end-to-end completion, these diagnostics examine the specific behaviors that task advancement is designed to support.

D.1 Benchmark Coverage of the Diagnostics

Field-level diagnostics require both an acquired value and an identifiable destination for its later use. We classify all 117 MobileWorld GUI-only tasks by the principal information requirement in their instructions and official definitions (Figure 4). The classification identifies which tasks support this diagnostic.

The census identifies 52 tasks whose principal requirement is to transfer acquired text or numerical content to a later GUI operation, comprising 47 multi-app tasks and five single-app tasks. Tasks involving final answers, decisions based on source information, file transfers, or navigation require different evaluation criteria. A source-to-target field test therefore applies to a particular information requirement, rather than to every multi-app task.

These 52 tasks define the benchmark scope of source-to-target field scoring. The main-text audit uses a reference catalogue covering 21 of them, comprising 14 fixed-role and seven collection tasks. Its 52 shared values provide identical field references across the five methods. The catalogue covers a subset of the applicable tasks.

D.2 Preserving Information beyond Its Source

We measure retention after information has entered state. This requires an identifiable acquisition followed by an opportunity to retain the value. We therefore track values that match both their cited read-only UI source and the state supplied to the actor. Instruction constants and echoes of the agent’s own input are excluded. This defines a diagnostic of acquired information with a verifiable textual source.

Scanning all 756 valid archived TAM-family episodes yields 202 bindings across 32 tasks, where a binding associates a task role with a value. These 32 tasks contribute every acquisition satisfying the above rule. The 198 bindings with subsequent decisions yield 3,751 value–decision pairs. Every later decision is scored, including those where the value has disappeared, regardless of episode success. Availability is the fraction of these pairs in which the value remains in state, averaged equally across tasks. It reaches 92.3% overall, 93.1% in an application different from the source, and 89.6% when the value is absent from both current XML and recent text (Figure 5).

For the temporal comparison, we require ten subsequent recorded decisions per binding so that every point follows the same values. Otherwise, episodes ending earlier would change the composition of the curve. All 106 bindings meeting this duration requirement enter the analysis, covering 24 tasks. Values remain in the denominator even when they disappear. After ten steps, 95.1% remain in state, compared with 57.6% present in current XML or recent text (Figure 6). These results show that TAM preserves acquired information across application changes and extended action sequences. Advancement State keeps earlier results available to later decisions even when they are absent from the current XML and recent text.

Scores measure literal retention in primary state, excluding quoted evidence. Observation ends with the episode. A value may disappear after replacement or completed work. The shared protocol specifies matching rules and longer follow-up windows.

D.3 Preparing Inputs for an Operation

We test whether state organization brings an operation’s source-derived inputs together before entry. The ten-task panel was chosen by task structure to cover cross-application dependencies, one-to-many coordination, document grounding, and terminal effects. Flat state retains facts and unfinished requirements while removing prerequisite links and associated action guidance. Both conditions disable persistent retrieval and learning. We examine all catalogued destination operations in this panel. Nine tasks contribute 23 fields grouped into ten operations. The remaining task requires a decision without field entry. Two saved revisions provide 20 operation instances.

An operation is prepared when all its audited, environment-derived target values appear together in state before the first entry attempt. TAM prepares 40% of operations versus 20% for flat state. Correct first entry requires all audited fields to be correct on their initial entry. Final accuracy allows repairs, reaching 40% and 35%, respectively (Figure 7(a)).

The shared-source comparison examines input organization in workflows where both agents encounter the required source information. All operations meeting this condition are included, yielding ten instances from five tasks across the two revisions, including invoice cases that both agents fail. TAM prepares 80% versus 40% for flat state and achieves correct first entry for 80% versus 50% (Figure 7(b)).

These ten instances contain the 18 field instances in the main-text paired analysis. Using the first entry after complete source exposure as the checkpoint gives the same results. Across the six multi-input instances, TAM prepares 66.7% versus 33.3% for flat state, while final correctness is 66.7% for both. The paired comparisons show the value of organizing facts around the operations that need them. TAM more often assembles inputs before entry and achieves more correct first attempts when both agents have encountered the source information.

D.4 Access to Captured Cross-Application Information

We test access to information already recorded in TAM’s state after an application change. The same questions compare reading this information from memory with recovering it from the interaction history.

A readout question requires a source-linked fact in state at a checkpoint in a different application from its source. This tests access to captured information after a context change. The archive yields 26 distinct eligible claims. A fixed-seed selector retains at most two per task to limit repeated contributions from one workflow, yielding 23 claims. We score all 20 with resolvable source references, spanning 13 tasks and 14 checkpoints, including an incorrect stored value. The claim selector does not inspect episode success or probe answers. Three claims have unresolved object, quantity, or temporal references. The shared protocol details the selection.

In each readout test, the same model answers the same question from the same current observation under five context conditions: TAM state, ordinary notes, full XML/action history, history with sampled images, and recent context. Notes are generated from the interaction prefix before the query is supplied, without access to TAM state or the reference answer. A query is correct only when every requested field matches its source-checked reference after format normalization. We average queries within each task before averaging across tasks, and also report the query mean.

TAM achieves the highest observed accuracy under both weightings (Table 8), with input size close to ordinary notes and 37.3% fewer input tokens than full textual history. Under the same task weighting, TAM state reduces readout error by 80.0% relative to notes, 50.0% relative to full textual history, and 66.7% relative to visual history. These are relative error reductions. TAM’s accuracy advantage is largest over recent context and ordinary notes (Figure 8).

The field-level breakdown distinguishes incomplete answers from incorrect derived values (Table 9). TAM, full textual history, and visual history achieve 100% field accuracy on multi-field queries, compared with 76.9% for notes. The additional errors under full and visual history concern derived times. All five contexts repeat one incorrect amount already present in the interaction prefix.

TAM combines accurate access to captured information with compact context. Its state supports more reliable cross-application readout than ordinary notes at a similar input size, while using substantially fewer input tokens than full textual history.

D.5 Quality of Local Learning Signals

We apply three policies to the same recorded candidate pools, retaining all candidates, retaining only candidates from successful episodes, or following TAM’s storage decisions. A candidate pairs a claimed local result with its interaction evidence. Tasks contribute through the learning candidates they produce. Each test includes all candidates meeting its reference conditions below. Correctness measures the quality of retained material, while coverage measures how much correct material is retained.

Local outcomes.

To assess local outcome judgments independently of terminal success, we include all 20 admitted proposals made without terminal evaluator feedback. Proposals nominated by the evaluator already use the terminal signal being compared and are accounted for separately. TAM’s retained outcomes are 100% supported and cover 83.3% of the supported pool (Figure 9(a)). Success-only selection gives 85.7% correctness. It admits premature completion claims from a workflow that succeeds later. TAM excludes these contradicted claims. Missing supported outcomes result from review-output processing failures, which remain included in the coverage calculation. Local verification thus improves the reliability of outcome evidence selected for operator learning.

Acquired values.

Value-level scoring compares a specified resource field with an external reference. Within the source-reference catalogue, we include every admitted field with a complete, unambiguous value claim and a determinate reference in benchmark fixtures, injected messages, or source documents. This yields 234 fields across 20 tasks, including correct and incorrect values. Incomplete claims and roles without resolved references remain in the full candidate accounting (Table 13).

To prevent candidate-rich tasks from dominating the comparison, we fix weights before selection so that each task contributes equally to the common pool. TAM retains 88.3% of correct material, compared with 64.3% for success-only selection. Correctness among retained values is 93.8% and 99.4%, respectively (Figure 9(b)). TAM combines higher retained-value correctness than keeping all candidates with broader coverage of correct material than success-only selection. This expands the evidence available for operator learning, including supported progress from unsuccessful workflows.

Sensitivity to repeated values.

Table 10 also gives equal weight to reference groups defined by task, resource role, and reference value. Correctness and coverage are ratios of weighted counts. Supported values remain in the coverage denominator even when their group retains none. TAM’s coverage advantage persists under both weightings, showing that the gain holds when either tasks or repeated source values receive equal weight. The shared protocol also reports the unweighted comparison.

D.6 Learning from Incomplete Workflows

We examine when correct local information first appears in workflows that ultimately fail. This timing question requires at least one source-checked correct record. We include every failed execution meeting this condition in the source-value audit, yielding 29 executions across 16 tasks. Records contribute whether or not they are retained for learning. Positions are normalized by the number of executed decisions, and tasks receive equal weight.

The median first-record position is 28.6% of execution, and 72.9% of audited executions contain a correct record by their midpoint (Figure 10). Correct material from 74.8% of these executions is eventually retained for learning. The dashed curve locates those retained records within their source workflows. The timing results show that useful learning material can arise early in a workflow that ultimately fails. TAM retains this partial progress for operator learning, extending the value of an execution beyond its terminal outcome. Table 11 breaks down retention and timing by information type.

Operators linked to 15 retained candidates subsequently appear in other tasks’ actor prompts. Their recorded lineage connects these deliveries to ten correct destination uses. The shared protocol accounts for all delivered cases. These traces document delivery and subsequent behavior, while the main-paper ablation evaluates persistent operators as a whole.

Figure 11 illustrates one such chain. The source correctly reads a sender’s number from a lunch invitation but fails to create the calendar event. Its operator is recalled for an interview invitation, where the actor reads a different number from a resume, enters it as the recipient, and completes the task. This chain demonstrates how supported progress from an incomplete workflow enters memory and becomes guidance for a different task.

D.7 Using Recalled Experience with New Inputs

We examine how recalled acquisition experience is used in a later task. A reuse opportunity begins when an operator reaches the actor. Scanning all 756 archived executions yields 206 such cases across 60 tasks, counting each operator once per execution. Of these, 165 concern information acquisition. We follow the first subsequent binding for the recalled resource, including incorrect and unresolved values. All 66 deliveries with such a binding enter the value audit, yielding 86 fields across 21 tasks. The other 99 deliveries remain in the coverage account. Task references support 65 of the 86 fields, contradict two, and leave 19 unresolved.

Adapting to changed values.

We test inputs that the target task requires the agent to obtain from the environment. Source and target must refer to the same information requirement and semantic field, with comparable value types. For example, a phone number is compared with a phone number, and an event’s start time with another start time. A changed reference distinguishes adaptation to the target task from repeating a source value. We include every field whose target reference differs from all comparable source values. Of the 24 qualifying fields, 20 match the new reference, one is incorrect, and three remain unresolved (Figure 12(a)).

From a binding to a destination.

Literal text entry links a recorded value to a destination control. We inspect every bound value matched to an executed text-entry action and check its destination in subsequent XML or screenshots. Of 29 matched fields, 23 (79.3%) reach the intended destination with the correct value (Figure 12(b)). One enters an incorrect value, one occurs only in an unrelated message-search field, and four lack a resolved reference. The correct uses span 22 actions in 22 episodes across seven tasks. Of the 23 correct field uses, 21 follow semantic guidance without an executable GUI route. The other 57 fields have no matching text-entry action and are outside this destination test, which does not cover other input modes such as time pickers. The two tests examine overlapping subsets of the same 86 fields. Together, the tests show that TAM combines reusable acquisition guidance with information obtained for the current task. The transfer traces demonstrate correct binding and destination use with new task values, supporting the reuse of experience across changing inputs.

D.8 Inference and Context Allocation

We examine how recorded inference is divided between the actor and additional model calls, and how much actor text is devoted to state and operator guidance. A shared actor prompt format gives the state-and-guidance block consistent boundaries, making its text share comparable across executions. We include every valid archived execution using this format, yielding 250 episodes across 96 tasks. Repeated executions are averaged within each task. The records include five archived memory settings, detailed in the shared protocol.

For each task, we average the fraction of recorded tokens used by additional model calls across its executions. Across tasks, the median is 1.7% (interquartile range 0.4–6.8%). For actor context, we first take the median fraction of prompt characters devoted to state and operator guidance within each execution, then average these episode medians within each task. The median across tasks is 5.7% (4.3–7.8%), as shown in Figure 13. This measure covers 7,107 saved actor prompts.

Across configurations, the median token share of additional model calls ranges from 0.5% to 13.4%, and the median text share from 4.1% to 6.3%.

These profiles show that TAM provides explicit task state and reusable guidance through a compact addition to actor context. The small median share of tokens used by additional calls complements this representation, supporting the practicality of integrating memory into ongoing execution.

Analysis Protocols and Sample Definitions

Sources and links to the main results.

The source labels in Table 12 distinguish benchmark metadata (B), historical executions (H), paired state controls (P), and fixed-checkpoint readout tests (Q). Historical executions cover multiple prompt and memory configurations. They document observed behavior under the recorded configuration of each episode. The paired state study holds its two arms within each saved revision, with persistent retrieval and learning disabled. The readout study holds questions and checkpoints fixed while varying the supplied context. Baselines use their fixed recorded trajectories. This panel measures attained information identification and use on common field references. These records are separate from the benchmark-level aggregation protocol.

Benchmark result identities.

The MobileWorld app-count table is a grouped view of the main-result register, and the Full TAM row in the ablation table uses the same Full TAM register. Diagnostic records retain their own source identities. Links to the main registers are made by exact episode identity, not merely by shared task identifiers. This structure connects the reported comparisons without conflating historical configurations.

References and units.

Field judgments combine benchmark definitions, source observations, executed actions, and destination observations. Audits are model-assisted and accompanied by their evidence. Unresolved judgments remain separate. Table 12 distinguishes tasks, episodes, operations, fields, and repeated observations within tasks.

Persistence and controlled state execution.

The fixed archive contains 756 valid full-memory executions across 115 tasks. Inclusion requires a value in its cited read-only UI source and in the actual actor state. This defines the 32-task acquisition cohort. Instruction constants and echoes of the agent’s own input are excluded. Typed matching covers email addresses, URLs, dates, times, phone numbers, and identifiers with at least seven digits. Other text requires eight alphanumeric characters. Every later prompt enters the score, including those missing the value. Cross-app decisions yield 2,509 pairs from 24 tasks. Absence from current XML and recent text yields 1,024 pairs from 22 tasks. Each condition includes all matching decisions. These are literal-presence measurements. Images and other prompt blocks are outside the immediate-text comparison. The temporal plot instead requires ten complete subsequent decisions per binding, yielding 106 bindings across 24 tasks. This duration criterion keeps the same values at every step and uses neither episode success nor subsequent retention. Longer follow-up requirements define separate cohorts. At 15 decisions, state and current XML/recent text contain 98.8% and 34.3% of tracked values (88 bindings, 20 tasks). At 20 decisions, the corresponding figures are 81.5% and 60.6% (67 bindings, 18 tasks). These endpoints use equal task weights within each cohort.

The paired state panel uses Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, temperature 0, and a 50-action limit. Both saved revisions use seed 7. The flat-state intervention includes associated guidance and output examples. Both arms disable persistent retrieval, writes, and learning. Section D.3 extends the main-text paired runs. Shared source exposure is determined after execution. Full-panel results accompany this conditional comparison.

Readout selection and inputs.

The selector scans 117 historical task records. The 53 first occurrences of a stored claim in a later application yield 32 occurrences with valid source and destination apps in declared multi-app tasks, or 26 distinct claims across tasks. Seed 20261003 and a cap of two claims per task select 23. Source review resolves 20, including one incorrect stored claim. Three have unresolved source-object, quantity, or temporal references. Thus the test concerns access to facts previously captured in TAM state.

All conditions use Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct at temperature 0. They share the current screenshot, XML, recent actions, task, and environment policy. An initial probe omitted the environment policy, including the device date. Corrected inputs were then applied to every condition with questions, references, and checkpoints unchanged. Only corrected responses enter this exploratory comparison. Visual history adds up to seven earlier screenshots. Query-blind notes use the full prefix and the same image sample, with a 128-word target. Reported tokens cover readout, excluding memory and note construction. Source-to-query gaps range from one to 11 steps, with median two.

Omitting each task in turn leaves an 8.3–16.7 percentage-point TAM advantage over notes and a 0–4.2 point difference from full history. These ranges measure sensitivity, not confidence intervals. Paired and field-error analyses reuse all 100 responses. The 28 requested fields are nested within 20 queries. The five multi-field queries contain 13 requested fields. Error categories describe returned values, not internal causes. For context cc, relative error reduction is 100​(Ec−ETAM)/Ec100(E_{c}-E_{\mathrm{TAM}})/E_{c}, where EE averages query errors within tasks and then equally across tasks. All contexts use the same questions and fixed weights. Error rates are 3.85% for TAM, 19.23% for notes, 7.69% for full history, 11.54% for visual history, and 73.08% for recent context. Relative reductions differ from percentage-point accuracy gains.

Candidate census and source references.

Of 756 valid executions, 751 match a retrospective review record by namespace and episode identifier. The 430 executions without candidates remain in the inventory. The other 321 produce 582 proposals across 48 tasks, including 120 outcomes and 462 resources.

Of 105 admitted outcomes, 85 nominated by native evaluation are excluded from the independent outcome test. All 20 remaining proposals are included. Two supported proposals fail source-validity normalization and three unresolved proposals have malformed review JSON. Among the 15 with usable review decisions, TAM stores ten supported outcomes and none of the five contradicted outcomes.

All 372 admitted resource candidates enter Table 13. Official task roles define 297 reference slots in 266 candidates. The 234 complete slots span 210 candidates and 146 executions. The 63 unresolved slots include missing dates, partial claims, and ambiguous source roles. Another 106 candidates lack static acquired-value references or concern instruction-given content. Unassessed items receive no correctness label. Field judgments assess recorded values, not every statement in an operator. The local-outcome panel uses all 20 eligible proposals. Unresolved retained items remain in its correctness denominator, and processing failures do not remove supported items from coverage. The source-value panel uses all 234 complete fields across 20 tasks. A field from task tt receives weight 1/nt1/n_{t}, with ntn_{t} fixed from that task’s complete fields before selection. Correctness divides retained supported weight by all retained weight. Coverage divides retained supported weight by all supported weight in the pool. Without weighting, TAM has 94.9% correctness and 78.2% coverage, versus 98.8% and 76.4% for success-only selection.

Timing and reuse of partial results.

All 41 reference-correct failed-source candidates have original proposal indices and complete logs, covering 29 executions across 16 tasks. Each task receives weight 1/161/16, divided equally among its qualifying executions. Execution progress is the one-based record position divided by the number of logged decisions. The median is the smallest observed fraction whose cumulative task weight reaches 50%. Final-decision records remain included.

Both curves use the same execution weights. The second curve uses the first correct record that is eventually retained, located at its original recording position. Executions without retained records contribute zero throughout. This curve describes the origin of retained material rather than the time of retrospective storage. Local correctness covers specified source values, not every claim in a learned operator.

Table 11 uses equal task weights within each information type. Material retention averages each task’s retained fraction of correct records. Execution retention and midpoint coverage average within-task execution fractions. Timing uses each execution’s first record of the relevant type. The overall row deduplicates executions. All eligibility rules are unchanged from the original source-value audit.

Of the 29 stored failed-source candidates, operators linked to 15 appear in 56 later episode–operator pairs across 26 tasks. Twenty pairs have a subsequent new binding, yielding 25 fields with 18 correct, two incorrect, and five unresolved values. Ten correct destination uses occur in ten executions. Each target unit is counted once despite multiple source contributions. This accounting connects checked source values, operator delivery, and subsequent behavior.

Reuse and computation.

Chronological reuse is checked within namespaces by matching retrieved operator identifiers to saved actor prompts. Across all 756 valid runs, 206 first episode–operator deliveries occur in 168 executions across 60 tasks. They comprise 165 acquisitions, 34 interface outcomes, and seven unresolved types. The first subsequent binding is fixed before scoring, preventing later repairs from replacing an incorrect initial value.

Changed-input eligibility uses target references, independently of target correctness. Comparisons require the same schema, semantic field, and value type. Compound source records are resolved to the matching field. The 86 target fields include 24 changed inputs, eight unchanged references, six inputs not newly acquired, and 48 without determinate comparisons. Destination scoring checks every literal-entry match against subsequent observations and permits repairs. The 57 unmatched fields receive no destination judgment. Other GUI input modes lie outside this test. Delivery and subsequent behavior are observed. Establishing the incremental benefit of a particular source contribution requires controlled memory-bank comparisons.

Of 784 valid archived executions, 250 from 96 tasks share the actor prompt format. All qualifying episodes contribute within-task averages. Token shares include repair calls. Character shares cover the state-and-guidance block, excluding earlier execution recall. The ledger also retains 214 infrastructure-invalid attempts and covers all 117 task identifiers.
